name: Node.js

foundation.via: A founding project, from the Node.js Foundation formed in 2015

summary: The JavaScript runtime for servers and command-line tools: Google’s V8 engine plus libuv’s event loop, so one thread serves many connections while I/O happens in the background.
intro: Node.js runs JavaScript outside the browser. It takes V8, the engine in Chrome, which compiles JavaScript to machine code as it runs and collects its garbage, and adds what a browser doesn’t have: files, sockets, processes, HTTP and a module system. Almost no function in its standard library blocks. A call such as `fs.readFile` or `http.get` starts the work and returns at once, and its callback or promise runs later. After running the main script, Node enters the event loop, implemented by the C library libuv, and exits when there are no callbacks left. Network I/O goes to the operating system’s own readiness APIs; work that has no asynchronous system call, such as file system operations, `dns.lookup()`, zlib and some crypto, runs in libuv’s thread pool, four threads by default (`UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE`).

Your JavaScript itself runs on one thread, so there are no locks to deadlock on, but a slow synchronous callback stalls every connection. CPU-heavy work goes to `worker_threads`, and `child_process` and `cluster` spread a server over several cores. Over the years the runtime has absorbed what used to need packages, such as a stable test runner (`node:test`) and, in 2026, a release-candidate `node:sqlite` module. It runs TypeScript files directly, stable since v24.12 and v25.2, by replacing type annotations with whitespace and refusing syntax that needs code generation, such as `enum`. `require()` can load ES modules without top-level `await`, and the `--permission` flag, stable since v22.13, restricts file, network, child-process and worker access as a seat belt for trusted code, not a sandbox for hostile code.

Releases are planned by the Release Working Group. Until now a major version came out every April and October, and only even-numbered ones got long-term support. On October 28, 2026, Node.js 26 entered Active LTS, supported until April 2029, with 24 (“Krypton”) in maintenance until April 2028 and 22 until April 2027; 20 reached end of life in April 2026. From Node.js 27 there is one major a year: an alpha from October, a Current release in April, then 30 months of LTS, so every version gets LTS.
strengths: Many concurrent connections on little memory: an idle socket costs a callback and some state, not a thread
One language across browser, server and build tooling, with npm’s registry of packages behind it
A broad standard library that now covers testing, TypeScript type stripping and a permission model without extra packages
Predictable support: 30 months of LTS per even-numbered line today, and for every line from Node.js 27
limits: One JavaScript thread per process: a heavy `JSON.parse`, regex or synchronous call blocks every request until it returns, so CPU work must move to worker threads or other processes
libuv’s thread pool has four threads by default, so many concurrent file, DNS lookup or zlib calls queue behind each other unless `UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE` is raised at start-up
Built-in TypeScript only strips types: no type checking, no `tsconfig` paths, no `enum` or decorators, and `.tsx` isn’t supported
The permission model doesn’t protect against malicious code; the docs say Node trusts any code it is asked to run, including every dependency

story: Ryan Dahl presented Node.js at JSConf EU in Berlin in November 2009, in a 45-minute talk that ended in a standing ovation. Servers of the time mostly handled concurrency with threads; he argued that network programs, which spend their time waiting on I/O, were better served by events and callbacks on one thread. He had tried Ruby, C and Lua first, but their libraries were built around blocking calls; server-side JavaScript had no such habits to unlearn, and its closures suited callbacks. A month after the talk Joyent hired Dahl, and the company became the project’s sponsor.

By 2014 many core contributors were unhappy with how Joyent ran the project and how slowly it shipped, and in late 2014 they forked it as io.js, which released faster and tracked newer V8 versions. The Linux Foundation brokered a settlement: the Node.js Foundation, launched on June 16, 2015, with IBM, Intel, Joyent, Microsoft and PayPal among its platinum members, gave the project neutral governance under a Technical Steering Committee. Node.js 4.0, in September 2015, merged the two codebases, adopted semantic versioning and introduced the LTS schedule that lasted a decade. In March 2019 the Node.js Foundation merged with the JS Foundation to form the OpenJS Foundation.

In 2026 the Release Working Group said that schedule had outlived its purpose: odd-numbered releases saw little use, the odd/even split confused newcomers, and security releases across four or five active lines had become hard for volunteers to sustain. Node.js 26 is the last line under the old model, and from Node.js 27 there is one release a year, with an alpha channel for breaking changes.

choices.choice: Non-blocking I/O everywhere, with one JavaScript thread
choices.why: Dahl meant Node for I/O-heavy network programs, where thread-based servers are inefficient and hard to use. If no library call blocks, one thread can wait on many sockets, and code never needs locks.
Server-side JavaScript had no blocking I/O libraries to unlearn, its closures suited callbacks, and browser developers already knew the language.
The fork showed that one company’s control could split the community. Moving the project into a Linux Foundation project with an open steering committee let the two sides merge their code.

choices.choice: One major release a year from Node.js 27
choices.why: Few people used the odd-numbered releases, and patching four or five lines at once overloaded volunteer releasers. One release a year, each with LTS, means fewer lines to patch and a simpler rule for users.

timeline.text: Ryan Dahl presents Node.js at JSConf EU in Berlin in November
Core contributors fork it as io.js late in the year
Node.js Foundation forms on June 16; Node.js 4.0 merges io.js in September
Becomes a founding project of the OpenJS Foundation on March 12
Running TypeScript by stripping types becomes stable (v24.12, v25.2)
Node.js 26 ships in May and enters LTS on October 28; Node.js 27 alpha begins under one-release-a-year
